questions.question: How do you use when().thenReturn() to stub a method in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito when thenReturn | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use when(mock.method(args)).thenReturn(value) to configure a mock to return a specific value when that method is called with those arguments. This is the fundamental stubbing pattern in Mockito. Set up the stub in the Arrange phase before executing the code under test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the core Mockito stubbing API and can write basic unit tests with mocked dependencies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Configuring the stub after calling the method under test, which means the mock returns null instead of the stubbed value
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show you know chaining multiple thenReturn calls for consecutive invocations and can switch to thenThrow or thenAnswer when needed

sections.title: Understanding Mockito Method Stubbing
sections.content: **when().thenReturn()** is the primary way to configure mock behavior in Mockito. When you create a mock object with @Mock or Mockito.mock(), all methods return default values (null, 0, false, empty collections). To make a mock useful, you **stub** specific methods to return controlled values. The pattern is: **when(mockObject.methodCall(args)).thenReturn(valueToReturn)**. This tells Mockito: "When this exact method is called with these arguments, return this specific value." Think of it like programming a robot: you're teaching the mock what to say when asked specific questions. The stub must be configured **before** you call the code that uses the mock, typically in the Arrange or Given phase of your test. This is the foundation of isolation testing — you control all inputs to focus on testing one class at a time.

sections.title: Basic Stubbing Example with Service and Repository
Key Points
content: **when()**: static method from Mockito class that starts the stubbing chain, accepts the method call you want to stub
**thenReturn()**: completes the stub by specifying what value to return when the stubbed method is called
**Argument matching**: by default uses equals() to match arguments; use argument matchers like any(), anyString() for flexible matching
**Stubbing order**: must configure stubs before the code under test runs, typically in the test setup or Arrange phase
**Multiple calls**: chain .thenReturn(val1).thenReturn(val2) or use thenReturn(val1, val2, val3) for consecutive calls
**Type safety**: the return type of thenReturn must match the method's return type or you'll get a compile error
**Overwriting stubs**: calling when().thenReturn() again on the same method replaces the previous stub

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When you're asked how to use when-then-return in Mockito, start with the syntax: you call when, pass in the method call on your mock object, then chain thenReturn with the value you want returned. So it's when-mock-dot-method-then-return-value. The purpose is to control what your mock returns so you can test your class in isolation. For example, if you're testing an OrderService that depends on an OrderRepository, you'd mock the repository and stub its findById method to return a specific Order object. That way you're not hitting a real database. You set up the stub in the Arrange phase before you call the service method. A common mistake freshers make is stubbing after they've already called the method under test, which means the mock just returns null. The stub has to be configured first. To show deeper understanding, you can mention that you can chain multiple thenReturn calls if the method gets called more than once and you want different values each time. You can also switch to thenThrow if you need to test error handling, or thenAnswer if the return value needs to be computed based on the input arguments.

questions.question: How do you stub a method to throw an exception in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito thenThrow Exception | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use when(mock.method()).thenThrow(new ExceptionType("message")) to make a mock throw an exception when that method is called. For void methods, use doThrow(new ExceptionType()).when(mock).voidMethod() because when-then syntax doesn't work with void returns. This lets you test error handling logic.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can test error scenarios and exception handling paths, which are just as important as happy path testing
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only testing the happy path and never verifying that exceptions are handled correctly when dependencies fail
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Combine thenThrow stubbing with assertThrows to verify your service layer catches, wraps, or propagates exceptions appropriately

sections.title: Testing Exception Scenarios with Mockito
sections.content: In production systems, things go wrong: databases become unavailable, networks fail, validation errors occur. **Testing exception paths** is critical but often overlooked. Mockito's **thenThrow()** lets you simulate these failure scenarios in unit tests. Instead of returning a value, you configure the mock to throw an exception when a method is called. This allows you to verify that your code handles errors gracefully: does it catch the exception? Does it wrap it in a custom exception? Does it clean up resources? Does it return a meaningful error response? The syntax is **when(mock.method()).thenThrow(new ExceptionType())** for regular methods. For **void methods**, you must use the do-family syntax: **doThrow(exception).when(mock).voidMethod()** because when-then doesn't work with void returns. You can throw checked exceptions (IOException, SQLException) or unchecked exceptions (IllegalArgumentException, NullPointerException) depending on what you're testing.

sections.title: Stubbing Exceptions for Service Layer Error Handling
Key Points
content: **thenThrow(exception)**: makes the stubbed method throw the specified exception when called, works with both checked and unchecked exceptions
**thenThrow(ExceptionClass.class)**: alternative syntax that creates the exception internally, useful when you don't need a custom message
**doThrow() for void methods**: required syntax for void methods because when-then doesn't support void returns
**Checked exceptions**: must be declared in the method's throws clause or you'll get a compiler error when stubbing
**Multiple exceptions**: chain thenThrow calls to throw different exceptions on consecutive invocations, useful for retry testing
**Testing exception handling**: combine with assertThrows from JUnit 5 to verify your code throws or catches the expected exception type
**Real-world scenarios**: common uses include simulating database failures, API timeouts, validation errors, and resource exhaustion

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To stub a method to throw an exception in Mockito, you use when-mock-dot-method-then-throw-new-exception. So if you're testing a service that calls a repository and you want to simulate the database being down, you'd write when-repository-dot-find-by-id-then-throw-new-data-access-exception. This lets you test that your service handles the error correctly, like wrapping it in a business exception or returning an error response. One important thing: for void methods, you can't use the when-then syntax because void methods don't return anything. Instead you use do-throw-when: do-throw-new-exception-dot-when-mock-dot-void-method. A common mistake freshers make is only testing the happy path where everything works. But in production, exceptions happen all the time, so you need to test those paths too. To stand out, you can show that you combine the stubbing with assert-throws from JUnit 5. So you stub the dependency to throw an exception, then assert that your service either propagates it or wraps it in a custom exception type. That shows you're thinking about error handling at the service layer.

questions.question: How do you use thenAnswer() for dynamic stubbing in Mockito?
questions.title: Mockito thenAnswer Dynamic Stubbing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: thenAnswer() accepts a lambda or Answer implementation that computes the return value dynamically based on the actual arguments passed to the method. Use when(mock.method(any())).thenAnswer(invocation -> compute(invocation.getArgument(0))) when the response depends on input values, unlike thenReturn which always returns the same static value.

interviewer_intent.testing: Advanced Mockito knowledge and understanding of when static stubbing is insufficient for realistic test scenarios
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to use multiple thenReturn calls with hardcoded values when the logic clearly depends on the input argument
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a concrete example like a save method that returns the entity with a generated ID, which is a very common pattern in repository testing

sections.title: Dynamic Stubbing with thenAnswer
sections.content: Sometimes **static return values aren't enough**. Imagine testing a save method that should return the same entity you passed in, but with an auto-generated ID. You can't use **thenReturn()** with a hardcoded value because the entity changes with each test. That's where **thenAnswer()** comes in. It accepts a lambda (or Answer implementation) that receives an **InvocationOnMock** object containing the actual arguments and method details. You can inspect the arguments, perform computations, and return a dynamic result. Think of it as a mini-function that runs every time the stubbed method is called. Common use cases: echoing input back with modifications (like adding an ID to a saved entity), computing results based on input (uppercase a string, multiply a number), returning different values based on argument type or content, or simulating complex stateful behavior. The lambda form is **thenAnswer(invocation -> { /* compute result */ })** where you access arguments via **invocation.getArgument(index)**.

sections.title: Dynamic Stubbing for Repository Save Method
Key Points
content: **thenAnswer(lambda)**: accepts a lambda that receives InvocationOnMock and returns the computed result, executed on every call
**invocation.getArgument(index)**: retrieves the argument at the specified position, cast to the expected type
**invocation.getArguments()**: returns all arguments as an Object array when you need multiple arguments
**Type casting**: you must cast the retrieved argument to the correct type, use generics to avoid ClassCastException
**Dynamic behavior**: perfect for simulating methods that transform input, generate IDs, or compute values based on arguments
**Stateful simulation**: can maintain state in the lambda's scope to simulate stateful dependencies like counters or caches
**Performance**: slightly slower than thenReturn because the lambda executes on every invocation, but negligible in unit tests

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Then-answer is for dynamic stubbing when the return value needs to depend on what arguments were actually passed to the method. With then-return, you give it a fixed value that's always returned no matter what. But with then-answer, you provide a lambda that gets executed every time the method is called, and it receives an invocation object that has the actual arguments. So you can inspect the arguments and compute a result. A classic example is stubbing a repository save method. When you save an entity, the repository should return that same entity but with a generated ID. You can't use then-return with a hardcoded entity because the input entity is different in each test. So you use then-answer with a lambda that grabs the input entity from the invocation, creates a new one with an ID, and returns it. The lambda form looks like: then-answer-invocation-arrow-get-argument-zero. You access arguments by their index, starting at zero. A common mistake is trying to use multiple then-return calls with different hardcoded values when the logic really depends on the input. That's a sign you need then-answer. Another use case is testing methods that transform input, like a service that converts strings to uppercase. You'd stub the dependency with then-answer to actually perform that transformation based on what string was passed in.

questions.question: What happens when a non-stubbed method is called on a Mockito mock?
questions.title: Mockito Default Return Values | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Mockito mocks return safe default values for non-stubbed methods: null for objects, zero for numeric primitives, false for booleans, and empty collections for collection types. This is the RETURNS_DEFAULTS answer strategy. No exception is thrown unless you enable strict stubbing mode.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Mockito's default mock behavior and that mocks are lenient by default
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting a NullPointerException or exception when a non-stubbed method is called, which doesn't happen with default mock settings
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the different answer strategies available: RETURNS_DEFAULTS, RETURNS_SMART_NULLS, RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS, and strict stubbing introduced in Mockito 2

sections.title: Understanding Mock Default Behavior
sections.content: When you create a mock with Mockito and call a method you haven't stubbed, you might expect an exception or error. **But Mockito returns sensible defaults instead.** This is called **lenient mocking** and it's designed to make tests less brittle. Object references return **null**. Numeric primitives (int, long, double) return **0**. Booleans return **false**. Collections (List, Set, Map) return **empty collections**, not null. Optionals return **Optional.empty()**. This behavior is defined by the **RETURNS_DEFAULTS** answer strategy. Why does Mockito do this? It allows partial stubbing — you only configure the methods your test actually uses, and other methods won't blow up. The downside is you might accidentally call a non-stubbed method and get null, leading to NullPointerException later in your test. To catch this, Mockito 2+ introduced **strict stubbing** mode (enabled by default with MockitoExtension) which warns about unused stubs and unnecessary stubbings.

sections.title: Observing Default Return Values from Mocks
Key Points
content: **RETURNS_DEFAULTS**: the default answer strategy that returns null for objects, 0 for numbers, false for booleans, empty for collections
**RETURNS_SMART_NULLS**: alternative strategy that returns special null objects that throw better error messages when methods are called on them
**RETURNS_DEEP_STUBS**: allows chaining method calls on mocks (mock.getUser().getName()) without explicitly stubbing intermediate calls
**Strict stubbing**: enabled by default in Mockito 2+ with JUnit 5, detects unused stubs and potential issues with stubbing configuration
**No exception by default**: calling non-stubbed methods does not throw exceptions in lenient mode, which can hide test configuration mistakes
**Interactions recorded**: even non-stubbed method calls are recorded and can be verified with verify(), allowing behavior verification
**When it matters**: this becomes important when your code doesn't check for null and you get NPE deep in the code under test

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When a non-stubbed method is called on a Mockito mock, it doesn't throw an exception. Instead, it returns safe default values. That's null for object types, zero for numbers, false for booleans, and empty collections for List, Set, or Map. This is what's called lenient mocking. The idea is that you only need to stub the methods your test actually cares about, and other methods won't cause failures. So if you're testing a service method that only calls find-by-id on a repository, you don't have to stub every other repository method. A common mistake freshers make is expecting a null-pointer-exception when they call a non-stubbed method. That doesn't happen. The mock just returns null, and then if your code tries to call a method on that null, that's when you get the NPE, but it's later in the execution. To show deeper knowledge, you can mention that Mockito has different answer strategies. RETURNS-DEFAULTS is the standard one. RETURNS-SMART-NULLS gives you better error messages by returning special null objects. And RETURNS-DEEP-STUBS lets you chain method calls without stubbing each level. Also, in newer Mockito versions with strict stubbing mode enabled, you'll get warnings if you have unused stubs, which helps catch configuration mistakes.

questions.question: How do you stub void methods in Mockito?
questions.title: Stubbing Void Methods
questions.direct_answer: Use doNothing().when(mock).voidMethod() to stub a void method that should do nothing, or doThrow(exception).when(mock).voidMethod() to make it throw an exception. The do-family syntax is required because when().thenReturn() doesn't work with void return types.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the do-star API family, which is necessary for void methods and also safer when working with Spies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to use when-mock-dot-void-method-then-return which doesn't compile because void methods have no return value
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention doAnswer as the most flexible option when you need custom logic executed when the void method is called, like capturing arguments or simulating side effects

sections.title: Stubbing Void Methods with the Do-Family API
sections.content: Void methods don't return values, so the **when().thenReturn()** syntax doesn't make sense. Mockito provides the **do-family API** specifically for void methods: **doNothing()**, **doThrow()**, and **doAnswer()**. The syntax is reversed: **doAction().when(mock).voidMethod(args)**. Most of the time, void methods on mocks do nothing by default, so you don't need to explicitly stub them with **doNothing()**. You use it mainly for clarity or when you want to explicitly document that a method should be called but have no side effects. The more common cases are **doThrow()** to test error handling when a void method fails (like a notification service throwing an exception), and **doAnswer()** to execute custom logic like capturing arguments or simulating side effects (like adding to a list). This API is also **safer for spies** because when-then syntax calls the real method during stubbing, which can cause unwanted side effects. With do-when, the real method is never invoked during stub configuration.

sections.title: Stubbing Void Methods with doThrow and doAnswer
Key Points
content: **doNothing()**: explicitly stubs a void method to do nothing, useful for clarity but often unnecessary since it's the default behavior
**doThrow(exception)**: makes the void method throw an exception when called, essential for testing error handling of void operations
**doAnswer(lambda)**: executes custom logic when the void method is called, useful for capturing arguments or simulating side effects
**Reversed syntax**: do-family methods use doAction-when-mock-method syntax instead of when-mock-method-thenAction
**Required for void methods**: when-then syntax doesn't compile with void methods because there's no return value to stub
**Safer for spies**: do-family methods don't invoke the real method during stubbing, preventing unwanted side effects on partial mocks
**Default behavior**: void methods on mocks do nothing by default, so explicit stubbing is only needed for exceptions or custom behavior

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To stub void methods in Mockito, you use the do-family API because when-then-return doesn't work with void methods. The syntax is reversed: you start with the action, then when, then the mock, then the method. So it's do-nothing-dot-when-mock-dot-void-method. Most of the time you don't actually need to stub void methods because they do nothing by default on mocks. But you use do-throw when you want to test error handling. For example, if you're testing a service that sends notifications and you want to simulate the email sender throwing an exception, you'd use do-throw-new-exception-dot-when-email-sender-dot-send. That lets you verify your service handles the failure correctly. The most flexible option is do-answer, which lets you execute custom logic when the void method is called. A common use case is capturing arguments. Say you have a logger dependency and you want to verify what was logged. You can use do-answer with a lambda that adds the logged message to a list, then assert the list contains what you expect. A common mistake is trying to use when-mock-dot-void-method-then-return-something, which doesn't compile. Another thing worth mentioning is that the do-family syntax is also safer when you're working with spies, which are partial mocks. With when-then, the real method gets called during stubbing, but with do-when, it doesn't, which avoids unwanted side effects.

questions.question: What is thenAnswer() and when do you use it?
questions.title: thenAnswer() in Mockito
questions.direct_answer: thenAnswer lets you compute a return value dynamically based on the actual arguments passed to the stubbed method. Use it when the response depends on input, like returning a saved entity with a generated ID or transforming the input argument.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the limitation of static stubbing and know when argument-dependent behavior is needed
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using thenReturn with hardcoded values when the test logic clearly depends on what input was passed to the method
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the lambda form with a concrete example: thenAnswer-inv-arrow-inv-dot-get-argument-zero-to-upper-case, demonstrating argument access and transformation

sections.title: When Static Stubbing Isn't Enough
sections.content: **thenAnswer()** bridges the gap between static and dynamic stubbing. With **thenReturn()**, you provide a fixed value that's always returned regardless of the input. This works for many scenarios, but sometimes the correct response depends on what arguments were actually passed. Imagine testing a service that calls a repository's save method. The repository should return the entity with a generated ID, but each test passes a different entity. You can't hardcode a single return value. Or consider a method that should echo back its input transformed in some way — uppercase a string, double a number, reverse a list. **thenAnswer()** solves this by accepting a lambda (or Answer implementation) that executes each time the stubbed method is called. The lambda receives an **InvocationOnMock** object with access to the actual arguments via **getArgument(index)**. You can then compute and return the appropriate result. This makes your tests more realistic and flexible while still maintaining isolation from real dependencies.

sections.title: Step 1: Identify When Input Determines Output
sections.content: Use **thenAnswer()** when the return value logically depends on the input arguments. Common scenarios: repository save methods that return the input entity with an ID added, transformation methods that modify input (uppercase, encoding, serialization), lookup methods where the result is derived from the key passed in, or stateful simulations where each call affects the next. If you find yourself trying to predict exactly what entity or value will be passed in each test and hardcoding multiple return values, that's a signal you need dynamic stubbing. Ask yourself: does the real method compute its result based on input? If yes, your stub should too. Another indicator is when you're using argument matchers like any() or anyString() but returning a fixed value — that mismatch suggests the stub should adapt to the actual argument.

sections.title: Step 2: Access Arguments and Compute Result
sections.content: The **InvocationOnMock** object passed to your lambda provides **getArgument(index)** to retrieve arguments by position (0-indexed) and **getArguments()** to get all arguments as an array. Cast the argument to the expected type. For example, **Customer customer = invocation.getArgument(0)** retrieves the first argument as a Customer. Then perform your computation: create a modified copy of the entity, apply a transformation, look up a value in a map, or increment a counter. Return the computed result. The lambda can be a single expression for simple cases: **thenAnswer(inv -> inv.getArgument(0).toString().toUpperCase())** or a full block for complex logic. You can even maintain state in the lambda's closure to simulate stateful dependencies like caches or counters. Just remember the lambda executes on every call, so keep it fast and simple.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Dynamic vs static**: thenReturn provides fixed values, thenAnswer computes values based on actual arguments passed to the stubbed method
**InvocationOnMock**: the object passed to the lambda, provides access to arguments, method details, and the mock itself
**getArgument(index)**: retrieves the argument at the specified position, returns Object so you must cast to the expected type
**Lambda form**: thenAnswer(inv -> expression) for simple cases, thenAnswer(inv -> { block }) for complex logic
**Common use cases**: repository save methods returning input with ID, transformation methods, lookups, and stateful simulations
**Type safety**: cast arguments carefully to avoid ClassCastException, use generics to make the cast explicit and safe
**Performance**: negligibly slower than thenReturn since the lambda executes on each call, but irrelevant in unit tests

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Then-answer is for when you need the mock to return different values based on what arguments are actually passed in, unlike then-return which always gives you the same static value. The classic example is testing a repository save method. When you save an entity, the real repository would return that entity but with a generated ID. You can't use then-return with a hardcoded entity because each test might save a different entity. So you use then-answer with a lambda that grabs the input entity from the invocation object, creates a new entity with an ID, and returns it. The syntax is then-answer-inv-arrow, where inv is the invocation object. You access arguments with inv-dot-get-argument-zero, which gets the first argument. You'd cast it to the entity type, then return a modified version. Another use case is transformation methods. Say you're testing a service that calls a utility to uppercase strings. You'd stub the utility with then-answer-inv-arrow-inv-dot-get-argument-zero-dot-to-upper-case. That way the stub actually performs the transformation based on the input string. You use then-answer when the behavior clearly depends on the input. If you find yourself trying to predict every possible input and creating separate stubs for each, that's a sign you should switch to then-answer. It makes your test more realistic because the mock behaves like the real dependency would, adapting to the input it receives.

questions.question: How do you stub the same method to return different values on consecutive calls?
questions.title: Consecutive Call Stubbing
questions.direct_answer: Use when(mock.method()).thenReturn(val1, val2, val3) or chain multiple thenReturn calls. The first call returns val1, second returns val2, third returns val3. After the last value, subsequent calls return the last value repeatedly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Mockito knowledge for testing scenarios involving retries, pagination, or stateful behavior across multiple invocations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling when-then-return multiple times on the same method thinking each will be applied, but only the last stubbing takes effect
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the retry pattern: first call throws an exception to simulate failure, second call returns success to simulate recovery

sections.title: Stubbing Multiple Return Values for Consecutive Calls
sections.content: Sometimes a method is called multiple times in a test, and you need different return values for each call. **Chaining thenReturn() calls** or using the **varargs form** lets you define a sequence of return values. The syntax is **when(mock.method()).thenReturn(val1).thenReturn(val2).thenReturn(val3)** or the shorthand **when(mock.method()).thenReturn(val1, val2, val3)**. The first invocation returns val1, the second returns val2, and so on. **After the last value, all subsequent calls return the last value** — there's no exception or error. This is incredibly useful for testing **retry logic**: the first call throws an exception (use thenThrow then thenReturn), the second call succeeds. Or for **pagination**: first call returns page 1, second call returns page 2, third call returns an empty page to signal the end. Or for **iterative algorithms** where each call produces the next state. You can even mix **thenReturn, thenThrow, and thenAnswer** in the same chain to simulate complex behavior patterns across multiple invocations.

sections.title: Testing Retry Logic with Consecutive Return Values
Key Points
content: **Varargs form**: thenReturn(val1, val2, val3) is shorthand for chaining multiple thenReturn calls, both produce the same behavior
**Sequential returns**: first call returns val1, second returns val2, subsequent calls after the last value return that last value repeatedly
**Mixing behaviors**: you can chain thenReturn, thenThrow, and thenAnswer in any order to simulate complex scenarios
**Retry testing**: common pattern is thenThrow on first call to simulate failure, thenReturn on second call to simulate recovery
**Pagination testing**: return pages of data sequentially, ending with an empty collection or null to signal no more data
**Last stubbing wins**: if you call when-then-return twice separately on the same method, only the last one takes effect — use chaining instead
**Verification**: use verify with times(n) to assert the method was called the expected number of times in your retry or loop logic

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: To make a mock return different values on consecutive calls, you chain then-return calls or use the varargs form. So it's when-mock-dot-method-then-return-value-one-dot-then-return-value-two, or the shorthand: then-return-value-one-comma-value-two-comma-value-three. The first time the method is called, it returns the first value. The second time, it returns the second value. After you run out of values, all subsequent calls just return the last value in the sequence. This is really useful for testing retry logic. A common pattern is to simulate a failure on the first call and success on the second. You'd do when-gateway-dot-process-payment-then-throw-new-exception-dot-then-return-success-response. That tests that your service correctly retries after a failure and succeeds on the second attempt. Another use case is pagination. You stub the repository to return the first page, then the second page, then an empty list to signal there's no more data. A mistake freshers often make is calling when-then-return twice separately on the same method, thinking both stubs will be used. But actually, the second call overwrites the first, so only the last stubbing takes effect. You have to chain them together. To show deeper understanding, you can mention that you can mix then-return, then-throw, and then-answer all in the same chain to simulate really complex behavior across multiple calls.

questions.question: What is the difference between when().thenReturn() and doReturn().when() and when should you prefer one over the other?
questions.title: when/thenReturn vs doReturn/when
questions.direct_answer: when-then-return evaluates the stubbed method during setup, which is safe for mocks but can cause issues with spies. do-return-when bypasses method evaluation during stubbing, making it necessary for spies and void methods. Use do-return-when for spies to avoid invoking the real method during stub configuration.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Mockito's two stubbing APIs and the subtle but critical difference in when the real method is invoked
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using when-then-return on a spy where the real method has side effects or throws exceptions during stubbing, causing unexpected behavior
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clearly explain why the real method is invoked with when-then stubbing on spies and demonstrate with a concrete example of a side effect

sections.title: Two Stubbing APIs and When the Real Method Is Called
sections.content: Mockito has two stubbing syntaxes: **when().thenReturn()** and **doReturn().when()**. They look similar but behave differently. With **when(mock.method()).thenReturn(value)**, Mockito **actually calls the method** to set up the stub. For pure mocks, this is fine because the method doesn't exist — it's generated. But for **spies** (partial mocks wrapping real objects), calling the method during stubbing invokes the real implementation. If that method has side effects (writes to a file, increments a counter, throws an exception), those happen during test setup, not during the act phase. **doReturn(value).when(mock).method()** solves this by **not invoking the real method** during stubbing. The real method is bypassed, and the stub is configured without side effects. Use **when-then** for pure mocks (it reads more naturally) and **do-return-when** for spies and void methods. The reversed syntax of do-family methods might look awkward, but it's necessary to avoid method invocation during stub configuration.

rows: Dangerous if method has side effects

sections.title: When to Use Each Stubbing Style
sections.content: Use **when().thenReturn()** by default for pure mocks created with @Mock or Mockito.mock(). It's the standard syntax, reads naturally from left to right, and is safe because mocks have no real implementation. Use **doReturn().when()** in three situations. First, when stubbing **spies** (@Spy or Mockito.spy()) where the real method has side effects or might throw an exception — you want to avoid executing that logic during test setup. Second, when stubbing **void methods**, because when-then doesn't compile with void returns. Third, when the real method has **preconditions** that aren't met during stubbing but will be met during the act phase — for example, a method that requires database state that isn't set up yet. In practice, if you see unexpected behavior during test setup (exceptions thrown, counters incremented, files written), switch from when-then to do-return-when. The reversed syntax is a small price for avoiding unintended side effects during stub configuration.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Method invocation difference**: when-then actually calls the method during stubbing setup, do-when bypasses the real method completely
**Pure mocks**: when-then is safe and preferred because mocks have no real implementation to invoke
**Spies**: do-when is required to avoid invoking the real method during stubbing, which could have unwanted side effects
**Void methods**: do-family syntax is required because when-then doesn't compile with void return types
**Side effects**: if the real method writes files, increments counters, or throws exceptions, use do-when to avoid these during setup
**Readability trade-off**: when-then reads naturally left-to-right, do-when syntax is reversed but necessary for safety in certain cases
**Best practice**: default to when-then for mocks, switch to do-when for spies or when you see unexpected behavior during test setup

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The difference between when-then-return and do-return-when is about when the real method gets called during stubbing. With when-mock-dot-method-then-return, Mockito actually invokes the method to set up the stub. For pure mocks, that's fine because there's no real implementation — it's all generated. But for spies, which wrap real objects, calling the method during stubbing means the real code runs during your test setup phase. If that method has side effects like writing to a file or throwing an exception, those happen before you even get to the act phase of your test. Do-return-when solves this by bypassing the real method during stubbing. The syntax is reversed: do-return-value-dot-when-mock-dot-method. It looks a bit awkward, but it guarantees the real method isn't called during setup. So when do you use each? For pure mocks, use when-then-return because it reads more naturally. For spies, use do-return-when to avoid side effects. A concrete example: imagine a spy on a service with a method that increments a counter. If you use when-then-return, the counter gets incremented during stubbing, which is not what you want. With do-return-when, the counter stays at zero until your test actually calls the method. Do-return-when is also required for void methods because when-then doesn't compile with void returns. The key insight is that when-then evaluates the method to set up the stub, while do-when skips evaluation and directly configures the stub.
